en: Points of Controversy The Great Fifty-Section The Fifteenth Chapter
The Discourse on the Accumulation of Karma:
Is karma one thing and the accumulation of karma another?
Yes, it is so.
Contact is one thing, the accumulation of contact is another;
feeling is one thing, the accumulation of feeling is another;
perception is one thing, the accumulation of perception is another.
Volition is one thing, the accumulation of volition is another;
consciousness is one thing, the accumulation of consciousness is another;
faith is one thing, the accumulation of faith is another.
Energy is one thing, the accumulation of energy is another;
mindfulness is one thing, the accumulation of mindfulness is another;
concentration is one thing, the accumulation of concentration is another.
Is knowledge one thing and the accumulation of knowledge another?
Is lust one thing and the accumulation of lust another?
…pe… Is lack of moral dread one thing and the accumulation of lack of moral dread another?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Is action one thing and the accumulation of action another? Yes.
Is the accumulation of karma co-nascent with karma?
One should not say so… [etc.
… Is the accumulation of karma co-nascent with karma?
“Yes,” [you say].

“Is the accumulation of karma that arises together with wholesome karma itself wholesome? You should not say so… [as before] … “Is the accumulation of karma that arises together with wholesome karma itself wholesome?”
“Yes,” you say.
“Is the accumulation of karma co-arisen with a deed associated with pleasant feeling itself associated with pleasant feeling?
You must not say so … [and so on] …

Is the accumulation of karma co-arising with an action associated with a painful feeling …pe… or with a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, itself associated with a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?
One should not say so …pe….
Is the accumulation of karma co-nascent with the karma?
Yes. Is the accumulation of karma co-nascent with unwholesome karma unwholesome? Yes.
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Is the accumulation of karma co-arising with an unwholesome action itself unwholesome? Yes.
Is the accumulation of karma co-arising with an action associated with pleasant feeling itself associated with pleasant feeling?
One should not say so …pe… [the same applies to] unpleasant feeling …pe…
Is the accumulation of karma (kammūpacaya) that arises together with an action associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling itself associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?
One should not say so… [as before]… Is the action co-arisen with consciousness? Is the action possessed of an object?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Is the accumulation of karma co-nascent with consciousness? Is the accumulation of karma accompanied by an object?
You should not say so …pe…
Is the accumulation of karma co-nascent with consciousness, yet the accumulation of karma is without an object? Yes.
Is karma co-nascent with consciousness, yet karma is without an object?
It should not be said thus… [as before] …Is karma co-nascent with consciousness? Is it the case that when consciousness ceases, karma ceases? Yes.
Is the accumulation of karma co-nascent with consciousness, such that when consciousness ceases, the accumulation of karma ceases?
One should not say so… [and so on] … Is the accumulation of karma co-nascent with consciousness, such that when consciousness ceases, the accumulation of karma does not cease?
“Yes,” you say.
“Is karma co-nascent with consciousness, yet when consciousness ceases, karma does not cease?
You must not say so… [and so forth].
Is there an accumulation of karma within karma?
Yes. Is that very same karma the accumulation of karma? No.
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Is there accumulation of karma within karma, and from the accumulation of karma is result produced? Yes.
Is that very action itself the accumulation of karma and the fruition of karma? One should not say so… [and so on]… Is there an accumulation of karma within the action,
and from that accumulation of karma does the fruition arise, such that the fruition possesses an object?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Then is the accumulation of kamma with an object?
You should not say so …pe…
Is the accumulation of karma without an object?
Yes. Is the result (vipāka) without an object?
It should not be stated thus … [as before] … Is action one thing and the accumulation of action another? Yes.
“Has it not been said by the Blessed One:
‘Here, Puṇṇa, someone performs a bodily formation that is both harmful and harmless; he performs a verbal formation that is both harmful and harmless...
he performs a mental formation that is both harmful and harmless. Having performed a bodily formation that is both harmful and harmless, having performed a verbal formation...’”
Having performed a mental formation, one is reborn in a world that is both afflicted and unafflicted.
Having been reborn in such a world, both afflicted and unafflicted contacts touch him.

Being touched by both afflicted and unafflicted contacts, he experiences both afflicted and unafflicted feelings—a mixture of pleasure and pain—just as is the case with human beings, some gods, and some beings in the states of deprivation.
"Thus, Puṇṇa, there is the arising of a being from a being; one is reborn according to what one does, and once reborn, contacts touch that which has been reborn.
In this way, Puṇṇa, I say: 'Beings are heirs to their own kamma.
Is this indeed a sutta?
“Yes.
Well then, it should not be said that “kamma is one thing and the accumulation of kamma is another.”
The Discussion on the Accumulation of Karma is finished.
This is the fifteenth chapter. Its summary verse (uddāna) is as follows:
Conditionality is established as dependent origination and as a temporal period.
A moment, a fraction of a moment, an instant;
the four taints are without taints;
the aging and death of supramundane phenomena are supramundane.
The attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling is supramundane;
the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling is mundane;
one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling might pass away.
That very path is the cause for rebirth among non-percipient beings;
the action is one thing, and the accumulation of action is another.
The Third Fifty.
Its summary verse:
Latent tendencies,
restraint,
The eon and the root are established.
